articles.title: ‘The Body’ Creator on the Dance Team’s Sexuality, What Happened to Grace and Whether God Is Real
articles.content: SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers for “ The Body ,” now streaming on Netflix . If you’re looking for clear answers about whether or not God is real in the world of “The Body” — Netflix’s spooky new drama series about mass hysteria originating from a Catholic school dance team — you’re not going to find them. “If we ever fully defined it, it would break the rule of the show,” says creator Quinn Shephard . “The show is meant to mimic faith, so there’s people who believe, there’s people who don’t and there’s people in the middle, like me, who are like, ‘I don’t know.’” But regardless of whether it’s the big man upstairs or just some devious teenage girls pulling the strings, “The Body” has a lot to say about faith and its role in the lives of young and sometimes queer girls. Shephard is a proud lesbian who was raised in the church and has stepped away from it without fully rejecting it, and the show’s up-and-down relationship with God is a product of that. At the beginning of “The Body,” a devout Catholic named Grace (Sofia Wylie) is the clear standout at dance team tryouts, much to the chagrin of some of the team’s more senior members, who roll their eyes at her rule-following innocence. Thus, she’s put through a bit of hazing: At a Halloween party at an abandoned convent, she’s pressured to take Ecstasy by Elise (Sara Boustany), the team’s co-captain and resident badass, as everyone jokingly perform a ritual meant to sacrifice her soul to the devil. But the devil doesn’t seem to know that they’re joking. Anya (Kristina Bogic), who is Elise’s co-captain and the most popular girl in school, notices that Grace has wandered off alone. Alongside Lisbeth (Geena Meszaros), an awkward new girl who got rejected from the team in favor of Grace, she finds Grace on the ground, convulsing until she passes out. Anya and Lisbeth decide to take her to a hospital, but on the way, Grace appears to die. Because Anya supplied the Ecstasy, she’s terrified she’ll get in trouble.

articles.title: Documentaries at the Oscars: A History of Breaking Out of Their Category — and What It Means for ‘You Can See Everything’
articles.content: A documentary is a film, too. But at the Oscars , it still hasn’t been fully embraced as one. One of the breakout hits of the awards season is A24 ’s insanely entertaining “ You Can See Everything ” from directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, which had a surprise world premiere at the Telluride Film Festival in September and opened in theaters Oct. 16, grossing nearly $80 million at the domestic box office through its fourth weekend. Many professional pundits and awards enthusiasts are predicting the film will make history as the first documentary feature to land a best picture nomination. So we looked at the history of nonfiction films at the Academy Awards to see which movies have been embraced by the various branches and categories (some now defunct) over the years and what that history says about the film’s chances. Three of them won statuettes. Of the 14 nominations nonfiction films have collected outside their own race since 2013 (the 85th ceremony), 10 have come in best original song. articles.title: Jensen Huang’s Biopic Feels Inevitable — The Right One Might Be Impossible
articles.summary: After "The Social Reckoning" stumbled at the box office and voter backlash over data centers dovetailed with awards buzz for "Artificial," any film about the former Nvidia exec would have to keep pace with a tech industry that’s changing by the day.
articles.content: Hollywood loves a visionary, especially one whose biggest gamble eventually made him a billionaire. But the trouble with making a biopic about a tech mogul actively shaping the future? That kind of story often refuses to sit still long enough to be told before ending in calamity. When it comes to Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang , any filmmaker hoping to get ahead of the microchip company’s uncertain next chapter may already be too late. Or is it still… too early? On Thursday, Nvidia announced that Huang had resigned as CEO and board member, effective immediately. And no reason was given for the departure: a rather extraordinary development for someone who helped build the company into one of the most powerful and lucrative forces in artificial intelligence. For Hollywood, it’s the kind of twist that practically demands a screenplay. Now there’s a corporate disaster — involving an alleged Chinese espionage operation and reports of multiple extramarital affairs — at the end of it. Hot dog! Still, it’s anyone’s guess whether that fiery conclusion can seem genuinely relevant by the time film and TV creatives get around to adapting it. The entertainment industry has spent much of 2026 demonstrating how difficult it is to dramatize Silicon Valley while the real people involved keep making headlines. Aaron Sorkin’s “ The Social Reckoning ,” for example, opened to just $5.5 million in North America . That’s a disappointing debut for the follow-up to David Fincher’s “The Social Network,” which won three Oscars including best adapted screenplay. articles.title: ‘Heartland’ Review: Jessica Chastain Rocks a Stetson and a Swagger for a Soapy Nashville Noir
articles.content: When a young relative goes missing, a jaded former country star returns to the industry that chewed her up in 'Country Strong' director Shana Feste's thriller, which can be gaudy fun, but eventually peters out. Misty Jones keeps her Grammy in the fridge, alongside a near-empty Tupperware of chicken broth and, well, not a whole lot else: A former country superstar turned burnt-out rural hermit, she more or less lives off what once was, but her memories don’t exactly nourish her. Peculiar details like these enliven “ Heartland ,” a missing-person mystery that returns writer-director Shana Feste to the Nashville milieu of her 2010 sophomore feature “Country Strong.” So does Jessica Chastain ‘s surprisingly brash, beery performance as Misty, whose no-bullshit demeanor serves her well when she must turn amateur detective, investigating the disappearance of a relative who happens to be a rising country star herself. Related Stories Gang Dong-won, Kim Go-eun to Star in Netflix’s 'The Twilight Between Us' From 'When Life Gives You Tangerines' Director, 'Queen of Tears' Writer Jason Statham and Guy Ritchie Reunite — Again — for Netflix Revenge Action Movie 'Dogfight' Fusing Southern-fried noir atmospherics with the sequinned kitsch of a Music City backstage melodrama, “Heartland” often hits the same undemanding guilty-pleasure groove as “Country Strong” — or indeed the six-season run of TV’s “Nashville” in the 2010s. What it isn’t, at nearly any point, is an effective thriller. Feste’s thin screenplay is heavily reliant on Chastain’s brio to sustain a quest that only narrowly makes sense on a moment-to-moment basis, and never gathers much intrigue — since the villains are all glaringly identifiable as such from the get-go, while Misty’s rough-diamond integrity is never in doubt. articles.title: ‘La Bola Negra’ Creatives Faced a Ticking Clock to Finish the Film for Cannes, but Waiting for Snow Almost Kept the Ending From Being Shot
articles.content: “ La Bola Negra ” editor Alberto Gutiérrez knew he was up against time — the plan was that they wanted to take the film to the Cannes Film Festival, and the deadline was March. Filming began in November, and Gutiérrez was editing the movie. But there was one problem. The film didn’t have its ending, and it was a pivotal scene. Directed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi (known as Los Javis ), the film, now playing in theaters, is based on an unfinished play of the same name written by Spanish playwright Federico García Lorca in 1936. Tragically, Lorca never got the chance to finish the play. He was shot dead by nationalist forces after being imprisoned at the beginning of the Spanish Civil War. He is rejected because he is gay. At the heart of his story is conflict, as he has to make choices in life and deal with his family. When he goes to the casino to plead his case, he denies he’s gay. He wakes up covered in snow. As is thematic with Lorca’s poems, snow means death. He hears his grieving mother and asks her for a second chance after realizing that he’s dead. articles.content: Kaylee Hottle’s older sister, Jasmine Hottle, will step in to complete the late Godzilla vs. Kon g actress’ final movie following her death at age 18 . Andy Mingo, the writer and producer of What Doesn’t Kill Us , recently told People that Jasmine will be taking over the role that was initially intended for Kaylee. In July, Kaylee died in a car crash in Maryland, her father, Joshua Hottle, confirmed in American Sign Language at the time. “Like Kaylee, Jasmine is deaf, and her involvement allows us to honor Kaylee’s memory while continuing the work she was going to be part of,” Mingo said of the upcoming project. articles.content: Meet Cookie, Sugar and Mondine! They are in a camp. But no, this is not a youth summer camp. They are part of the resistance. In fact, they are part of a group of Gen Z volunteers in the jungles of Myanmar who try to endure 45 days of makeshift training in a top-secret camp before they go to the front line and face the military junta. Between drills, the young men, until recently students, teachers and tour guides, call home – or sing along to pop songs. Now, you can follow their transformation from civilians into soldiers in White Tiger Column , a new documentary that gets its world premiere in the International Competition of the International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam ( IDFA ), which runs through Nov. 22, to open the festival on Friday. The young men’s fight is for democracy. But its end is not in sight. Roberts died peacefully at his home in Los Angeles on Wednesday surrounded by his family after a brief battle with glioblastoma. articles.content: The ratings renaissance for Dancing With the Stars has continued throughout this season, and it reached a high with Tuesday’s episode. The episode, which featured the contestants and their pro partners dancing to Grammy-winning and -nominated songs — and live performances from Sheryl Crow, Maren Morris and Brandy and Monica — averaged 7.39 million viewers on ABC and Disney+ in Nielsen’s final same-day ratings. articles.content: TheWrap Screening Series: Marcellus Cox and four fellow filmmakers discuss their shorts and how it’s “the greatest time” for DIY movie-making It’s been a big year for short films. Two of the dominant names in the 2026 conversation, Curry Barker and Kane Parsons , both used YouTube as their stomping grounds, making microbudget shorts on their own until their big breaks with “ Obsession ” and “ Backrooms ,” respectively. It’s a moment of validation for those who have been grinding away at moviemaking on their own, a sign that filmmakers no longer need permission to get their starts. “I think it’s the greatest time for filmmakers, because you don’t have to worry about … dealing with the studios,” filmmaker Marcellus Cox told TheWrap on Wednesday during our Oscar-Qualifying Shorts Showcase. “Now, you control your own domain. articles.content: T.J. Power stars in this oddball Netflix exclusive, about a lonely middle-aged man whose life is ruined by a friendly alien he met in the ’90s The makers of “E.T. The Extra-Terrestrial,” “The Chronicles of Narnia” and “The Care Bears” probably meant well when they told children magical fantasies about befriending magical creatures and going on adventures, but those stories all have a problem. After the wonderment ends those kids have to go back to their normal lives. They have to put up with people who say aliens don’t exist, there’s no such thing as an enchanted wardrobe, and that bears don’t talk or shoot happiness lasers out of their chests. It’s fun to imagine getting superpowers, fighting monsters and saving the world. It’s scary to imagine going back to your homework and house chores afterwards. That’s enough to drive a normal person mad, and that’s what Daley Pearson and Jeffrey Walker’s “Allen” is about. T.J. Power stars as Petey, who met a cute space alien as a child and formed a deep, personal bond with the creature. When the alien, named Allen, gets pulled back into his mothership and whisked away, Petey spends the next 30 years trying to contact Allen in outer space. He’s afraid to move out of his childhood house in case Allen comes back and can’t find him. He doesn’t have a job, a goal or any meaningful relationships. He’s trapped in the past, unable to imagine a future that doesn’t revolve around his childhood escapism. “Allen” paints nostalgia as a trap, irresponsibly sprung on little kids, who eventually lose their ability to imagine a life outside of the box. articles.content: Peacock ‘s latest limited series “The Good Daughter” adds to the streamer’s solid run of women-led thrillers, though it’s best to interpret that label loosely. Then came a slight pivot into pulpy book adaptations with “Apples Never Fall” (2024) an adaptation of Lianne “Big Little Lies” Moriarty’s novel of the same name that was showrun by Melanie Marnich and centered around a wealthy family’s missing mom, played by Annette Bening. articles.content: It appears that Marvel has assembled a team of earth’s mightiest screenwriters to shape its most epic blockbuster yet . The Writer’s Guild of America has added the full list of writers who worked on “ Avengers: Doomsday ” to its directory , and comic book movie fans are already scanning it for clues about the film ‘s contents. For one thing, the credits erase all doubts that Deadpool and Wolverine will appear in the film, as both Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman are listed as providing additional literary material for the film. Reynolds was a writer on 2024’s Deadpool & Wolverine,” but this is actually Jackman’s first official writing credit listed in the WGA directory. But the Guild’s database also lists writers who did behind-the-scenes work on the script. A whopping eight writers received that “additional literary material” credit: Reynolds, Jackman, Eric Pearson, Chris McKenna, Erik Sommers, Jeff Loveness, Andrew Lanham, and Destin Daniel Cretton. The large list of writers is understandable when you consider how many characters “Doomsday” has to cover. articles.title: Saoirse Ronan Has Wanted to Direct Since She Was a Kid, and Her Exquisite First Short ‘Paper Plane’ Proves She’s Got the Goods
articles.summary: In her first and only interview since winning Best Narrative Short at the Austin Film Festival (and earning Oscar-qualifying status for her directorial debut), Ronan tells IndieWire about the joyous (and occasionally scary) process of moving into what could be a brand-new career for her.
articles.content: Like all great directors, Saoirse Ronan has the multitasking thing down pat. Earlier this week, IndieWire exclusively spoke with Ronan as she was walking around London during a particularly “crazy busy” time in her life (yes, we asked about Sam Mendes’ Beatles films , and Ronan could only smile and note that she couldn’t share a thing about them at this moment). Headphones on, jacket collar up, Ronan was getting her steps in while also talking about something she’s wanted to do for a very long time: direct a film . Earlier this month , Ronan’s “ Paper Plane ” won Best Narrative Short at the Austin Film Festival after debuting at Venice earlier in the season. Any win is nice, but a win at an Oscar-qualifying festival like Austin comes with an added sweetener: The film is instantly eligible for Oscar consideration for the 2027 ceremony. Jumping behind the camera is something Ronan has wanted to do for years, and her first offering (which she also wrote) is exquisite. When we first meet Fay, she’s launched a silent protest, announcing to her mother (via a titular paper plane message) that she will not return to their home until her father, who we instantly understand is a toxic presence, leaves for good. As Fay and her trusty dog sit it out in a grassy lot across the street from the family home, Ronan’s film unfolds with grace and honesty, ending on a heart-stopping note. articles.content: The Cinema Eye Honors have revealed nominations for the 20th annual awards ceremony. articles.title: ‘Ebenezer’ Review: Johnny Depp Is Absolutely Insufferable in a Dull and Dreary Christmas Carol
articles.summary: Ti West's horror-inflected take on Dickens' classic has a few nice flourishes, but Depp's muggy performance torpedoes the whole thing from the start.
articles.content: A Sauvage and jowly overactor in dire need of career rehabilitation could hardly ask for a better part to play than Ebenezer Scrooge. He’s a cruel miser of a man who comes to learn the error of his ways over the course of a ghost story that preys upon Christian precepts of redemption and forgiveness (along with the more secular warm and fuzzies of seeing a bad guy discover the joys of being good). Indeed, what is “ cancel culture ” if not a shackled delusion that visits self-made pariahs in the dead of night, and what is Charles Dickens’ “A Christmas Carol” if not a plea to believe that even the most odious of souls are still capable of being saved? articles.title: After ‘Whalefall’ Flops, Can Imagine Entertainment Return to Box Office Glory with ‘How to Rob a Bank’?
articles.summary: The production banner founded by Ron Howard and Brian Grazer is trying to make the kind of big screen hit that first solidified it as a major Hollywood player.
articles.content: “ How to Rob a Bank ” may benefit from doing just that. With career-low reviews for director David Leitch, the Amazon MGM Studios release has been tracking poorly and now looks unlikely to crack $10 million from 2,810 theaters in its domestic debut. For the film’s production banner, Imagine Entertainment , it is shaping up to be a second theatrical non-starter after its high-concept survival thriller “ Whalefall ” — about a scuba diver trapped in the belly of a marine mammal — got beached after its October opening with just a $39 million total worldwide despite solid reviews. Neither “How to Rob a Bank” nor “Whalefall” marks an auspicious wide release homecoming for Imagine, even if Amazon and Disney, respectively, fronted the budget and marketing spend on the films. That’s practically an epoch for Imagine, which was founded by Ron Howard and Brian Grazer and spent its early years asserting itself as a theatrical force with hits like “Kindergarten Cop,” “Liar, Liar,” “The Nutty Professor,” and Howard’s own films, like “Apollo 13” and “How the Grinch Stole Christmas.” A spokesperson for the banner declined to comment for this report. The company’s biggest hit after 2010 was the 2016 Dan Brown adaptation “Inferno,” which, at $220 million global, earned less than half the gross that its 2009 predecessor “Angels & Demons” did.
